en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 12.
Pārivāsikakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Those Undergoing Parivāsa)
1. The Duties of One Undergoing Probation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, monks undergoing probation were accepting the salutation from regular (pakatatta) monks.

Rising to meet [him], joining one’s palms, performing respectful duties, offering a seat, offering a bed, providing water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-washing stone, receiving the bowl and robe, and massaging the back during bathing.
Those monks who have few desires... [as before] ...they grumble, complain, and spread it about, saying:
“How indeed can monks who are on probation consent to the formal salutation,
rising up in respect, joining of palms, reverential salutation, offering of a seat, offering of a bed,
water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-stand, the receiving of bowl and robes, and the massaging of the back during bathing by regular monks?”
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One had the community of bhikkhus assembled and questioned the bhikkhus:
"Is it true, bhikkhus, that bhikkhus who are on probation consent to being saluted by bhikkhus who are in good standing?"
“Rising to meet [the teacher], joining one’s palms in salutation, performing acts of courtesy, offering a seat, offering a bed,
water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-stand, receiving the bowl and robes, and massaging the back during bathing?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is unbecoming, monks...
How indeed, monks, could monks on probation consent to [being treated as equals by] regular monks?”

Prostration, rising to greet, joining the palms in salutation, performing respectful duties, offering a seat, offering a bed, water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-washing stone, receiving the bowl and robes, and massaging the back during bathing.
Monks, this does not lead to the inspiration of those without faith... [and so on].
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Monks, a monk who is on probation must not consent to [the following].”
The paying of homage, rising up, and joining of palms in salutation toward regular bhikkhus.
Proper conduct,
the offering of a seat,
and the offering of a bed.
Water for washing the feet,
a footstool, a foot-washing stone,
and the receiving of the bowl and robes.
Bathing and back-massage:
whoever should consent to these, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow monks who are on probation to salute one another according to seniority and to rise for one another.

"Monks, I allow those monks who are on probation to perform five acts according to seniority: the act of joining the palms in salutation, the act of rising from one's seat in greeting, the offering of a seat, the offering of a bed, and the massaging of the back during bathing, as well as the providing of water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-washing slab, and the receiving of their bowl and robe."
The Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the rainy-season robe, the meal offering, and the meal itself.
Therefore, monks, I will lay down the proper conduct for monks who are on probation, as it should be observed by monks who are on probation.
Monks, a monk who is on probation must conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
one should not grant full ordination,
nor should one give formal support (nissaya).
A novice should not be attended upon;
the appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs should not be accepted;
and even one who has been appointed should not instruct the bhikkhunīs.
One must not commit the same offense for which the saṅgha has granted probation, nor another of a similar nature, nor one more serious than that;
the formal act is not to be criticized, nor are those who performed the formal act to be criticized.
One should not suspend the Uposatha of a regular monk,
nor should one suspend his invitation for the Pavāraṇā,
nor should one issue a formal command to him.
One should not initiate a formal reprimand,
one should not grant leave [for a legal procedure],
nor should one accuse [another].
He is not to be reinstated,
nor should he be associated with the monks.
Monks, a monk who is on probation must not walk in front of a regular monk.
One must not sit in front [of a regular monk].
Whatever belongs to the Saṅgha—the limit of seats, the limit of beds, or the limit of dwellings—should be assigned to him, and he should accept it.
Monks, a monk who is on probation must not have a regular monk as his attendant or walk ahead of him.
The attendant monk may visit families,
but he must not undertake the forest-dweller’s practice,
nor must he undertake the alms-food-eater’s practice.
And he should not have almsfood brought out on that account, thinking,
"Lest they should recognize me. Monks, a monk who is on probation should inform an incoming monk,
and he should inform an incoming monk.
It should be announced on the Uposatha day;
it should be announced on the Pavāraṇā day.
If one is ill, it should be announced even by means of a messenger.
“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence with monks to a residence without monks, except together with a regular monk (pakatatta) or except when there are obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence with monks to a non-residence without monks, except together with a regular monk or except when there are obstacles.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence with monks to either a residence or a non-residence without monks, except together with a regular monk or except when there are obstacles.”
“Monks, a monk who is on probation must not go from a non-residence with monks to a residence without monks, except together with a regular monk (pakatatta) or except when there is an obstruction.
Monks, a monk who is on probation must not go from a non-residence with monks to a non-residence without monks, except together with a regular monk or except when there is an obstruction.

Monks, a monk who is on probation must not go from a non-residence with monks to either a residence or a non-residence without monks, except together with a regular monk or except when there is an obstruction.”
“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a residence that has no monks, except with a regular monk or if there is an obstruction.
Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a non-residence that has no monks, except with a regular monk or if there is an obstruction.”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a residence or non-residence that has no monks, except with a regular monk (pakatatta) or except when there are obstacles.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence that has monks to a residence that has monks where the monks belong to a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka), except with a regular monk or except when there are obstacles.”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence with monks to a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except in the presence of a regular monk or except due to obstacles.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence with monks to a residence or a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except in the presence of a regular monk or except due to obstacles.”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except in the presence of a regular monk (a *pakatatta*) or except due to an obstacle.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a non-residence with monks to a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except in the presence of a regular monk or except due to an obstacle.”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks, or from a residence with monks to a non-residence with monks, where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except in the presence of a regular monk or in the event of an obstruction.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence with monks or a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except in the presence of a regular monk or in the event of an obstruction.”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence or non-residence with monks to a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different community, except in the presence of a regular monk or except due to an obstacle.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should not go from a residence or non-residence with monks to a residence or non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to a different community, except in the presence of a regular monk or except due to an obstacle.”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a residence where there are monks to a residence where there are monks, provided that those monks belong to the same community, if he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a residence where there are monks to a non-residence where there are monks, provided that those monks belong to the same community, if he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a residence where there are monks to a residence where there are monks, or to a non-residence, where there are monks belonging to the same communion, if he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a non-residence where there are monks to a residence where there are monks, where there are monks belonging to the same communion, if he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”
“Monks, a monk on probation should go from a non-residence with monks to a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same communion, if he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.

Monks, a monk on probation should go from a non-residence with monks to a residence or a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same communion, if he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”

“Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a residence that has monks who belong to the same community, if he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.

Monks, a monk who is on probation should go from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a non-residence that has monks who belong to the same community, if he knows: ‘I am able to go this very day.’”

"Monks, a monk who is on probation may go from a residence or non-residence that has monks to a residence or non-residence that has monks who belong to the same community, provided he knows: 'I am able to go there this very day.
Monks, a monk who is on probation must not dwell under one roof with a regular monk in a residence, nor must he dwell under one roof with a regular monk in a non-residence."
One should not dwell in a residence, whether it be a formal dwelling or not, under the same roof as one who is fully ordained.
Upon seeing a fully ordained monk, one must rise from one’s seat.
One should invite the fully ordained monk to sit.
A regular monk should not sit on the same seat as one;
nor, when seated on a low seat, should he sit on a high seat;
nor, when [the other] is seated on the ground, should he sit on a seat.
One should not walk on a walking path that is too narrow;
one should not walk on a high walking path while another is walking on a low walking path;
nor should one walk on a walking path while others are walking on the ground.
“Monks, a monk who is on probation should not [stay] together with a more senior monk who is also on probation...
nor with a monk subject to being sent back to the beginning...
nor with a monk subject to the *mānatta* penance.”

A bhikkhu who is practicing *mānatta* should not dwell under one roof in a residence with a bhikkhu who is practicing *mānatta*, nor should he dwell under one roof in a non-residence with a bhikkhu who is deserving of rehabilitation (*abbhānāraha*).
One should not dwell in a residence or a non-residence where there is only one roof-covering;
one should not sit on the same seat,
nor should one sit on a high seat while another is seated on a low seat.
One should not sit on a seat when one is seated on the ground;
one should not walk on a walking path when another is walking on a single walking path;
nor should one walk on a high walking path while another is walking on a low walking path.
One should not walk up and down on a walking path that is not designated as a walking path.
Monks, if one who is himself on probation should grant probation, or send back to the beginning, [together] with a fourth person who is also on probation...
One should grant the *mānatta* penance;
one who has completed twenty days of that should be rehabilitated. This is invalid and should not be done.
The ninety-four rules regarding the duties of one on probation are concluded.
Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, how many interruptions of the night are there for a monk who is on probation?
“Upāli, there are three interruptions of the night for a monk who is on probation:
living together [with others], being separated [from his companions], and failing to announce [his status].”
“Upāli, these are the three ways in which the night of a monk on probation is cut short.
Now at that time, a great community of monks had gathered in Sāvatthī.
The monks on probation were unable to complete their probationary period.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to set aside the probation.
And furthermore, monks, it should be set aside in this way.”

That monk who is on probation, having approached another monk, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having sat down on his heels, and having extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
“I set aside my probation.
His probation is then set aside.
‘I relinquish the formal act.
Thus the probation is relinquished.
Now at that time, the monks in Sāvatthī departed here and there.
The monks who were undergoing probation were unable to complete their probation.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to undertake probation.”
And furthermore, monks, it should be undertaken in this way:
that monk who is on probation should approach another monk, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit down on his heels, raise his joined palms, and say to him:
"I undertake the probation."
The probation has been undertaken.
[Thinking] “I undertake the duties,” the probation has been undertaken.
The duties for one undergoing probation are finished.
2. The Duties for One Subject to Be Sent Back to the Beginning.
Now at that time, monks subject to being sent back to the beginning consented to [the presence of] regular monks.

Saluting, rising up, joining the palms, performing respectful duties, offering a seat, offering a bed, water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-washing stone, receiving the bowl and robe, and massaging the back during bathing.
Those monks who have few desires... [as before] ...they grumble, complain, and spread it about, saying:
“How indeed can monks deserving of being sent back to the beginning consent to the formal salutation, rising up for, [and so forth] … the massaging of the back during bathing by regular monks?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that monks deserving of being sent back to the beginning accept from regular monks salutations, rising to greet them... [and so on] ...and having their backs rubbed while bathing?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is unbecoming...
How indeed, monks, could those monks who deserve to be sent back to the beginning consent to the salutation, the rising up... and the massaging of the back during bathing by regular monks?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].”
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Monks, a monk who is subject to sending back to the beginning should not consent to [the formal act].”
The paying of homage, rising up, and joining of palms in salutation toward bhikkhus who are of pure conduct.
Proper conduct,
offering a seat,
and offering a bed.
Water for washing the feet,
a footstool, a foot-washing stone,
and the receiving of the bowl and robes.
“Bathing and massaging the back:
whoever should consent to these, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, I allow monks who are subject to being sent back to the beginning to greet one another according to seniority, to rise for one another, and so forth … bathing and massaging the back.”
“I allow, monks, for those monks deserving to be sent back to the beginning, five things according to seniority:
the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the rainy-season robe, the meal-offering, and the meal.
Therefore, monks, I shall prescribe the proper conduct for those monks deserving to be sent back to the beginning, as to how those monks deserving to be sent back to the beginning should behave.”
"Monks, a monk who is subject to being sent back to the beginning must conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
he must not confer full ordination."
One should not give dependence,
one should not have a novice attend to oneself,
and one should not accept the appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs.
Even if he has been authorized, a monk must not exhort the bhikkhunīs.
He must not commit the same offense for which he was made subject to *mūlāya-paṭikassanā* by the Saṅgha, nor another offense of a similar nature, nor one more serious than that;
nor should he criticize the formal act.
The officiants are not to be censured.
One should not suspend the Uposatha of a regular monk,
nor should one suspend his Pavāraṇā.
One should not address him with a formal admonition,
nor should one initiate a censure against him,
nor should one demand an opportunity for a formal act.
He is not to be exhorted,
he is not to be reminded,
and he is not to be associated with by the bhikkhus.
“Monks, a monk who is subject to being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) should not walk in front of a regular monk (pakatatta),
nor should he sit in front of him.
Whatever constitutes the limit of the Saṅgha’s seats, the limit of the beds, or the limit of the dwellings, that must be given to him, and he must accept it.”
“Monks, a monk who is subject to sending back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) should not approach families with a regular monk as his forerunner or his follower,
nor should he undertake the forest-dweller’s practice (āraññikaṅga).”
The practice of eating only almsfood is not to be undertaken,
nor should one have almsfood brought out for that reason, thinking,

"Lest they should recognize me. Monks, a monk who is subject to being sent back to the beginning should not go from a residence with monks to a residence without monks, except with a regular monk or except when there are obstacles.

“Monks, a monk deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāya-paṭikassanāraha) should not go from a residence with monks to a non-residence without monks, except with one who is a regular member (pakatatta), except if there are obstacles.

Monks, a monk deserving to be sent back to the beginning should not go from a residence with monks to a residence or a non-residence without monks, except with one who is a regular member, except if there are obstacles.
Monks, a monk deserving to be sent back to the beginning should not go from a non-residence with monks to a residence without monks … [and so on].”

A monastery without resident monks may be visited …pe… a monastery with resident monks or a non-monastery without resident monks may be visited, except for a regular monk and except in cases of obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is subject to being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) must not go from a monastery with resident monks or a non-monastery to a monastery without resident monks …pe…
One may go to a non-residence that has no monks...
one may go to a residence or a non-residence that has no monks, except with a regular monk and except when there are obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is subject to being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) must not go from a residence with monks to a residence with monks... [and so forth].
A monastery with monks may be approached; ...

a monastery with monks or a non-monastery with monks may be approached where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except for one who is a regular member [of the same communion], and except when there is an obstacle.
Monks, a monk deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) should not go from a non-monastery with monks to a monastery with monks; ... [and so forth].
One may go to a non-residence that has monks …pe… one may go to a residence or a non-residence that has monks,
provided that there are monks belonging to a different community (nānāsaṃvāsaka), except for those who are regular members (pakatatta) and except in cases of obstacles.
Monks, a monk deserving to be sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanāraha) should not go from a residence or a non-residence that has monks to a residence that has monks …pe…
A monastery with monks may be approached …pe… a monastery with monks or a non-monastery with monks may be approached,
where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except for one who is a regular member [of the same communion], and except in the event of obstacles.
Monks, a monk deserving to be sent back to the beginning may approach a monastery with monks from a monastery with monks …pe…
From a non-residence that has monks...
[and so on] ...to a residence or non-residence that has monks where there are monks belonging to the same community, he should go if he knows: "I am able to go this very day.
Monks, a monk who is subject to being sent back to the beginning should go from a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks... [and so on].

A residence with monks... [as before] ...a residence with monks or a non-residence with monks, where there are monks belonging to the same community; a monk who is subject to being sent back to the beginning should go, O monks, to a residence with monks or a non-residence with monks... [as before] ...if he knows: "I am able to go this very day.
A monk who is subject to being sent back to the beginning should go, O monks, from a residence with monks or a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks... [as before].
A non-residence with monks...
[and so on] ...a residence or a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same community; if one knows:
"I am able to go this very day," then, monks, a monk who is subject to sending back to the beginning should not dwell under the same roof as a regular monk.
One should not dwell under one roof in a non-residence;
nor should one dwell under one roof in either a residence or a non-residence.
Upon seeing a regular monk, one should rise from one's seat.
A regular bhikkhu should be invited to sit on a seat;
one should not sit on the same seat as a regular bhikkhu;
nor, while sitting on a low seat, should one sit on a high seat.
One should not sit on a seat when one is seated on the ground;
one should not walk on a walking path when another is walking on a single walking path;
nor should one walk on a high walking path while another is walking on a low walking path.
One should not walk up and down on a walking path that one who is to undergo *mūlāyapaṭikassanā* (sending back to the beginning) must walk upon.
Monks, a monk who is to undergo *mūlāyapaṭikassanā* should not [walk] together with a monk who is on *parivāsa*...
nor should he walk together with a monk senior to him who is to undergo *mūlāyapaṭikassanā*.

A monk who is subject to the trial period (mānatta) must not dwell under one roof in a residence with a monk who is also subject to the trial period, nor with a monk who is practicing the trial period,
nor with a monk who is subject to rehabilitation (abbhāna).
One should not dwell under one roof in a non-residence;
nor should one dwell under one roof in either a residence or a non-residence;
nor should one sit on a single seat.
One should not sit on a high seat when seated on a low seat,
nor should one sit on a seat when the other is seated on the ground;
one should not walk back and forth on the same walking path.
One should not walk on a walking-path while another is walking on a low walking-path; one should walk on a high walking-path while another is walking on a low walking-path.
One should not walk on a walking-path while another is walking on the ground.
Monks, if one were to grant probation with a monk deserving of sending back to the beginning as the fourth member of the assembly, [that would be invalid].
If one were to send him back to the beginning,
grant him the *mānatta* penance,
and then rehabilitate him after he has completed twenty days— that would be an invalid act and not to be performed.”
The duties for one deserving to be sent back to the beginning are finished.
3. The Duties for One Deserving the Trial Period (Mānatta).
Now at that time, monks deserving the trial period consented to the salutation of regular monks.

Rising to meet him, saluting with joined palms, performing proper etiquette, offering a seat, offering a bed, providing water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-washing stone, receiving his bowl and robe, and massaging his back while he bathes.
Those monks who have few desires... [as before] ...they grumble, complain, and spread it about, saying:
“How indeed can monks who deserve the *mānatta* penance consent to the formal salutation,
rising up, joining of palms, respectful service, offering of a seat, offering of a bed,
water for washing the feet, a footstool, a foot-scraper, receiving of bowl and robe, and the massaging of the back during bathing by regular monks?”
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… “Is it true, bhikkhus, that bhikkhus deserving the *mānatta* discipline consent to the formal salutation, rising up in respect, … and the massaging of the back during bathing by regular bhikkhus?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is unbecoming...
How indeed, monks, could monks who are subject to the *mānatta* penance consent to being saluted by regular (*pakatatta*) monks... [and so on] ...or having their backs massaged during bathing?
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:”
“Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* penance must not consent to the salutation or the rising up in respect of regular monks.”
... [as before] ... massaging the back while bathing.
Whoever should consent to this, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“I allow, monks, for monks who are subject to the *mānatta* discipline, mutual salutation according to seniority, rising for one another... [and so on] ...and back-massage while bathing.
I allow, monks, for monks who are subject to the *mānatta* discipline, five things according to seniority:
the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*), the offering of food (*oṇojana*), and the meal.”
Therefore, monks, I will lay down the proper conduct for monks who deserve the *mānatta* penance, as it should be observed by those monks deserving *mānatta*.
Monks, a monk deserving *mānatta* must conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
He should not be ordained... [and so on] ...
(it should be expanded in the same manner as the sending back to the beginning).
He should not associate with the bhikkhus.
“Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* penance must not walk in front of a regular (*pakatatta*) monk,
nor sit in front of him.
Whatever constitutes the limit of seats for the Saṅgha, the limit of beds, or the limit of dwellings, that must be assigned to him, and he must accept it.”
Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline must not approach families with a regular monk as his attendant before or after him,
nor should he undertake the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññika-aṅga*).
The practice of eating only almsfood is not to be undertaken,
nor should one have almsfood brought from there for that reason, thinking,

"Lest they should recognize me. Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline should not go from a residence with monks to a residence without monks, except together with a regular monk or except when there are obstacles.

“Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline must not go from a residence with monks to a non-residence without monks, except with a regular monk (*pakatatta*) or except when there are obstacles.

Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline must not go from a residence with monks to a residence or a non-residence without monks, except with a regular monk or except when there are obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline must not go from a non-residence with monks to a residence without monks … [and so on].”
One may go to a non-residence that has no monks...
one may go to a residence or a non-residence that has no monks, except with a regular monk and except when there are obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline must not go from a residence or a non-residence that has monks to a residence that has no monks... [and so forth].
One may go to a non-residence that has no monks … one may go to a residence or a non-residence that has no monks, except with a regular monk (pakatatta) and except in the event of obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline must not go from a residence with monks to a residence with monks … [and so forth].
One may go to a non-residence that has monks … one may go to a residence or a non-residence that has monks,
provided there are monks there who belong to a different communion, except for one who is a regular member (*pakatatta*), and except in cases of obstacles.

A monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline should go, O monks, from a residence with monks or a non-residence with monks to a residence with monks... [and so on].

[and so on] ...a residence or a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same community; [in such a place], a monk who deserves the *mānatta* discipline should know: "I am able to go there this very day.
Monks, a monk deserving *mānatta* should not dwell under one roof in a residence together with a regular (*pakatatta*) monk.
One should not dwell under one roof in a non-residence;
nor should one dwell under one roof in either a residence or a non-residence.
Upon seeing a regular monk, one should rise from one’s seat.
A regular bhikkhu should be invited to sit on a seat.
One should not sit on the same seat as a regular bhikkhu;
nor, while sitting on a low seat, should one sit on a high seat.
One should not sit on a seat when one is sitting on the ground;
one should not walk on a walking-path when there is another walking-path;
and one should not walk on a high walking-path while another is walking on a low walking-path.
One should not walk back and forth on a walking path where one who is to walk back and forth is already walking.
Monks, a monk deserving of the *mānatta* discipline should not [walk] together with a monk on probation...
nor together with a monk deserving of being sent back to the beginning... nor together with a monk deserving of the *mūlāyapaṭikassanā* (sending back to the beginning).
One should dwell in a residence under one roof with a senior monk who is subject to the *mānatta* penance, ...
[and so on] ... with a monk who is practicing the *mānatta*, ...

The duties for one deserving the *mānatta* penance are finished.
4. The Duties for One Practicing the *Mānatta* Penance.
Now at that time, monks practicing the *mānatta* penance consented to being saluted by regular (*pakatatta*) monks.

Rising to meet [the teacher], joining the palms in salutation, performing acts of respect, offering a seat, offering a bed, providing water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone, receiving the bowl and robes, and massaging the back during bathing.
Those monks who have few desires... [as before] ...they grumble, complain, and spread it about, saying:
“How can monks who are undergoing the *mānatta* penance consent to the formal salutation, rising up in respect, and so forth, as well as the massaging of the back during bathing, from regular monks?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this connection, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that monks undergoing the *mānatta* discipline consent to the salutation, the rising to greet, and so forth, up to the massaging of the back during bathing by regular monks?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is improper,
monks … How indeed, monks, could monks undergoing the *mānatta* discipline consent to the salutation of regular monks … [and so on] … even the massaging of their backs while bathing? This, monks,
does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence …” [and so on].
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu undergoing the *mānatta* discipline must not consent to [certain things].”
The paying of homage, rising up, and the joining of palms in salutation toward regular bhikkhus.
Proper conduct,
the offering of a seat,
and the offering of a bed.
Water for washing the feet,
a footstool, a foot-washing stone,
and the receiving of the bowl and robes.
“Bathing and massaging the back:
whoever should consent to these, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
I allow, monks, for monks who are practicing the *mānatta* penance, mutual salutation according to seniority, rising up for one another... [and so on] ...bathing and massaging the back.”
"I allow, monks, for monks who are practicing the *mānatta* penance five things according to seniority:
the *uposatha*, the *pavāraṇā*, the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*), the feeding of guests (*oṇojana*), and meals.
Therefore, monks, I shall prescribe the proper conduct for monks who are practicing the *mānatta* penance, as it should be observed by those monks."
“Monks, a monk who is practicing the mānatta penance must conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
he must not confer full ordination.”
One should not give formal support (nissaya),
one should not have a novice attend upon oneself,
and one should not accept the appointment as an instructor of bhikkhunīs.
Even if authorized, a monk should not exhort the nuns.
He must not commit the same offense for which the Saṅgha has granted him the *mānatta* penance, nor another of a similar nature, nor one more serious than that;
nor should he criticize the formal act.
The officiants are not to be censured.
One should not cancel the Uposatha of a regular monk,
nor should one cancel his Pavāraṇā.
One should not issue a formal admonition,
nor initiate a censure, nor demand an opportunity for a defense.
He is not to be exhorted,
not to be reminded,
and he is not to be associated with by the monks.
“Monks, a monk who is practicing the *mānatta* penance must not walk in front of a regular (*pakatatta*) monk,
nor sit in front of him.
Whatever belongs to the end of the Saṅgha’s seating, bedding, or dwellings should be assigned to him, and he should accept it.”
Monks, a monk who is practicing the *mānatta* discipline should not approach families with a regular monk as his attendant before or behind him,
nor should he undertake the forest-dweller’s practice (*āraññika-aṅga*).
The practice of eating only almsfood (piṇḍapātikaṅga) need not be undertaken,
nor should almsfood be caused to be brought out for that reason, thinking, "Lest they recognize me.
A monk who is observing the penance (mānatta), monks, should announce his arrival to any visiting monks.
It should be announced to a visitor;
it should be announced on the Uposatha day;
it should be announced at the Pavāraṇā ceremony.
It must be announced every day.
If he is ill, it may be announced even by messenger.

Monks, a monk who is practicing the *mānatta* discipline must not go from a residence where monks are present to a residence where no monks are present, except with the Saṅgha or except in the event of obstacles.
“Monks, a monk who is practicing the *mānatta* penance should not go from a residence with monks to a non-residence without monks, except with the Saṅgha or except due to obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is practicing the *mānatta* penance should not go from a residence with monks to a residence or a non-residence without monks, except with the Saṅgha or except due to obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is practicing the *mānatta* penance should not go from a non-residence with monks to a residence without monks … [and so forth] …”
One may go to a non-residence that has no monks...
one may go to a residence or a non-residence that has no monks, except with the Saṅgha, except in the event of obstacles.
Monks, a monk who is practicing the *mānatta* penance must not go from a residence or a non-residence that has monks to a residence that has no monks... [and so forth].
A monastery without monks may be visited …pe… a monastery with monks or a non-monastery without monks may be visited, except in the company of the Saṅgha or except due to obstacles.

a monastery with monks or a non-monastery with monks may be gone to, where there are monks belonging to a different communion, except for the sake of the Saṅgha or except due to obstacles.

monks, a monk practicing the *mānatta* penance should go from that residence or non-residence with monks to a residence with monks …pe…
A non-residence with monks...
[and so on] ...a residence or a non-residence with monks where there are monks belonging to the same communion; [in such a place], one should know: "I am able to go this very day.
Monks, a monk undergoing the *mānatta* discipline must not dwell under the same roof as a regular (*pakatatta*) monk in a residence that is covered by a single roof.
One should not dwell under one roof in a non-residence;
nor should one dwell under one roof in either a residence or a non-residence.
Upon seeing a regular monk (pakatatta), one should rise from one’s seat.
A regular bhikkhu should be invited to sit on a seat.
One should not sit on the same seat as a regular bhikkhu;
nor, while sitting on a low seat, should one sit on a high seat.
One should not sit on a seat when one is sitting on the ground;
one should not walk on a walking path when another is walking on a single walking path;
nor should one walk on a high walking path while another is walking on a low walking path.
One should not walk back and forth on a walking path where one who is walking back and forth is already doing so.
Monks, a monk undergoing the *mānatta* discipline should not [walk] together with a monk on probation...
nor with a monk subject to being sent back to the beginning... nor with a monk subject to being reintegrated from the beginning.

A monk who is subject to the *mānatta* discipline must not live under the same roof as a monk who is also subject to the *mānatta* discipline and is senior to him; nor must he live under the same roof as a monk who is practicing the *mānatta* penance and is senior to him;
nor must he live under the same roof as a monk who is subject to rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) and is senior to him.
One should not dwell under one roof in a non-residence;
nor should one dwell under one roof in either a residence or a non-residence;
nor should one sit on a single seat.
One should not sit on a high seat when seated on a low seat,
nor should one sit on a seat when the other is seated on the ground;
one should not walk up and down on the same walking path.
One should not walk on a walking-path while another is walking on a low walking-path; one should walk on a walking-path while another is walking on a high walking-path.
One should not walk on a walking-path while another is walking on the ground.
Monks, if one were to grant probation with the one undergoing the *mānatta* penance as the fourth member, [that would be invalid].
If one were to send him back to the beginning,
grant him the *mānatta* penance,
and then rehabilitate him after he has completed twenty days, that would be an invalid act and not to be carried out.”
Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, how many interruptions of the nights are there for a bhikkhu who is practicing the *mānatta* penance?”
“Upāli, there are four ways in which the night of a monk practicing the *mānatta* penance is broken:
living together [with regular monks], being separated [from other monks], failing to announce [one’s status], and wandering in a group smaller than the required number.
These, Upāli, are the four ways in which the night of a monk practicing the *mānatta* penance is broken.”
Now at that time, a great community of monks was assembled in Sāvatthī.
The monks who were undergoing the *mānatta* penance were unable to complete it.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to set aside the *mānatta* penance.
And furthermore, monks, it should be set aside in this way:
That monk who is practicing the *mānatta* should approach one monk, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit in the kneeling position, raise his joined palms, and address him thus:”
‘I relinquish the mānatta.
The mānatta is thus relinquished.
‘I relinquish the duties. The duties are thus relinquished.
“The period of penance has been laid down.
Now at that time, the monks in Sāvatthī departed here and there;
thus, the monks who were practicing the penance were able to complete their penance.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to undertake the *mānatta* penance.
And furthermore, monks, it should be undertaken in this way:”

That bhikkhu who is practicing the *mānatta* penance should approach one bhikkhu, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, sit in the kneeling position with his hands joined in *añjali*, and say to him:
“I undertake the *mānatta*. Thus the *mānatta* is undertaken.
‘I undertake the duties,’ thus it is undertaken as the *mānatta* penance. The duties for one practicing the *mānatta* penance are finished.
5. The Duties of Those Eligible for Rehabilitation Now at that time, monks eligible for rehabilitation consented to the salutation, rising up in respect, and so forth,
as well as the massaging of the back during bathing, by regular monks.
Those monks who were of few desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can monks deserving of rehabilitation consent to the formal salutation, rising up in respect, and so forth, as well as bathing and back-massage from regular monks?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:

“Is it true, monks, that monks deserving of rehabilitation consent to the salutation, rising up in respect, and so forth, up to the massaging of the back during bathing, from monks who are in good standing?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“It is unbecoming...

How, monks, can monks deserving of rehabilitation consent to the formal salutation, rising up in respect, and so forth, as well as the massaging of the back during bathing, from monks who are in good standing?
“Monks, this does not lead to the inspiration of those without faith...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:”
“Monks, a monk deserving rehabilitation should not consent to saluting or performing services for monks who are of regular standing.
…pe…
“Bathing and back-massage:
whoever should consent to these, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
I allow, monks, for those monks deserving rehabilitation, mutual salutation, rising up in greeting according to seniority... bathing and back-massage.”
"I allow, monks, for monks who are deserving of rehabilitation, five things according to seniority:
the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the rainy-season robe, the meal offering, and the meal.
Therefore, monks, I shall prescribe the proper conduct for monks deserving of rehabilitation, as it should be observed by those monks."
“Monks, a monk who is worthy of rehabilitation should conduct himself properly.
In this regard, this is proper conduct:
he should not confer full ordination... [and so forth] ...”
(As above, so it should be expanded.
He must not associate with the regular monks.
Monks, a monk deserving of rehabilitation must not walk in front of a regular monk.
He must not sit in front [of regular monks].
Whatever belongs to the Saṅgha—the limit of seats, the limit of beds, or the limit of dwellings—must be given to him, and he must accept it.
Monks, a monk deserving rehabilitation must not have a regular monk as his attendant or walk ahead of him.
One may approach families accompanied by a junior monk as an attendant;
one should not undertake the forest-dweller’s practice;
one should not undertake the alms-food-eater’s practice.
And he should not have almsfood brought out on that account, thinking, "Lest they recognize me.
Monks, a monk deserving of rehabilitation should not go from a monastery with monks to a monastery without monks, except with one who is a regular member (*pakatatta*) or except due to an obstacle.
Monks, a monk deserving of rehabilitation should not go from a monastery with monks to a non-monastery without monks, except with one who is a regular member or except due to an obstacle. …
... [as above, it should be expanded in detail] ...
Monks, a monk who is deserving of rehabilitation should go from a residence where there are monks ... [as above].
Non-residences … [and so on] … whether a residence or a non-residence, a residence with monks … [and so on] … a non-residence with monks … [and so on] …
Whether it be a residence with monks or a non-residence, where there are monks who belong to the same communion, one should go only if one knows: "I am able to go this very day.
Monks, a monk deserving of rehabilitation must not live under the same roof as a regular monk in a residence, nor must he live under the same roof as a regular monk in a non-residence.
One should not dwell in a residence or a non-residence where one is covered by the same roof;
upon seeing a regular monk, one must rise from one’s seat,
and the regular monk should be invited to take a seat.
A regular bhikkhu must not sit on the same seat with one who is not regular;
nor, while sitting on a low seat, may he sit on a high seat;
nor, while [the other] is sitting on the ground, may he sit on a seat.
One should not walk on a walking path while another is walking on the same one;
one should not walk on a high walking path while another is walking on a low one;
nor should one walk on a walking path while another is walking on the ground.

“Monks, a monk deserving rehabilitation should not [dwell] together with a monk who is on probation … nor with a monk deserving to be sent back to the beginning … nor with a monk deserving the trial period.”
A monk who is practicing *mānatta* should not live under the same roof as a senior monk who is eligible for rehabilitation (*abbhāna*); he may live under the same roof in a monastery,
but he must not live under the same roof in a non-monastery.
One should not dwell in a residence or a non-residence that is covered by a single roof;
one should not sit on the same seat,
nor should one sit on a high seat while another is seated on a low seat.
One should not sit on a seat when one is seated on the ground;
one should not walk on a walking path when another is walking on a single walking path,
nor should one walk on a high walking path while another is walking on a low walking path.
One should not walk back and forth on a walking path that is not a designated walking path.
Monks, if one who is deserving of probation were to grant probation with a person deserving of sending back to the beginning as the fourth member, [that probation would be invalid].
One should grant the *mānatta* penance;
one who has completed that [period] should be rehabilitated. This is not a valid legal act, nor is it to be carried out.
The duties for one deserving rehabilitation are concluded.
The Second Chapter on Those Undergoing Probation (Pārivāsikakkhandhaka).
In this chapter there are five cases.
Its summary (uddāna) is as follows:
Those on probation perform salutations and rising up for monks who are in good standing.
And the joining of palms in respectful salutation.
Offering a seat, a bed, a footstool,
a bench, and a foot-washing stand;
When the bowl was being washed, the virtuous ones complained about the preparation;
there is an offense of wrong-doing for one who consents to it.
The five things to be done according to seniority:
the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā,
the rainy-season robe, and the meal of fresh food.
And the proper conduct therein for one who is going toward being a regular monk,
and whatever constitutes the limit.
Pure afterwards, and likewise [before];
the bringing of forest alms,
and for a guest on the Uposatha day.
On the invitation day, one may go by messenger;
one should go to where there are monks.
And the ordination must take place under a single roof.
And likewise one should invite them:
at a low seat, while walking,
or on the ground while walking.
Non-action by one who is senior,
the interruption of the night, and purification; laying down [the robe] and undertaking [it].
As with one on probation,
so it is for one deserving to go back to the beginning,
and likewise for one undergoing the period of penance (mānatta).
The method for those deserving rehabilitation,
and again the method for causing schism;
the three [cases] regarding those on probation.
In the four cases of practicing the *mānatta* penance,
they do not agree regarding the interruption of the nights,
nor regarding the daily [reckoning] during the *mānatta*.
Two types of actions are similar; the remaining three types of actions are both equal and similar.
The Pārivāsikakkhandhaka is concluded.
